idiom_name: abstract Mediator::notify(const Event&) + Colleague holding Mediator&
implementation_notes: The textbook structure maps directly: an abstract Mediator with one notify() entry point, a concrete mediator that owns or references the concrete colleagues, and a Colleague base storing a Mediator& so participants report events instead of calling peers. For a hub that only fans notifications out, a vector of std::function callbacks is lighter and needs no inheritance, and the library variants already implement that plumbing; write the classic form when the coordination rules are the design's centre of gravity and should be explicit and testable.
pitfalls: A Colleague that stores Mediator& must not outlive the hub; make ownership explicit (hub owns colleagues, or colleagues outlive the hub) rather than relying on reference lifetime.
notify(const Event&) with a string or enum payload gives up type safety; a closed event variant keeps the protocol compile-time checked.
The concrete mediator must know every colleague type, so adding a participant edits the hub - that is the growth path to a god object, so plan for it.

variants.name: Boost.Signals2 managed signals and slots
variants.idiom_name: boost::signals2::signal<void(const Event&)> members as the hub
variants.implementation_notes: Replace the abstract mediator with signals: the hub class exposes boost::signals2::signal members, colleagues connect lambdas or bound member functions and call operator() to emit, and the library tracks connections and disconnects automatically when a tracked object is destroyed - precisely the lifetime bookkeeping hand-written hubs get wrong. Slots run synchronously in connection order, so the coordination logic lives in ordinary slots and the Colleague base class disappears. Prefer it in non-GUI code where the hub is fan-out plus light routing; keep the classic structure when the coordination itself is the design.
pitfalls: Connections to plain lambdas are untracked: for a member function, connect a shared_ptr-tracked object or use a scoped_connection, or the slot outlives its owner.
With several slots the signal's return value is produced by the template's combiner; a void signal is the right choice for a mediator hub, otherwise the combined result surprises callers.
Signals2 is thread-safe for connect/disconnect, but emission is synchronous and re-entrant: a slot that emits the same signal recurses.

variants.name: Qt signals/slots with a QObject hub
variants.idiom_name: QObject hub: colleagues emit signals, QObject::connect() expresses the rules
variants.implementation_notes: In Qt the mediator is an ordinary QObject - typically the dialog or controller: widgets emit signals, the hub connects them to slots that implement the interaction rules, and no widget holds a pointer to another. QObject::connect() with the function-pointer syntax is compile-time checked, and Qt removes connections automatically when either end is destroyed, so the classic lifetime problem is the framework's job. Use it whenever Qt is already in the stack; a hand-written mediator pays off mainly in Qt-free code or where the hub must be tested without an event loop.
pitfalls: Connections are direct and synchronous by default, so a blocking slot stalls every colleague; use Qt::QueuedConnection or a worker thread for slow work.
Connecting to a lambda without a context object keeps the connection alive past the receiver's owner; pass a context (usually this) so Qt disconnects it.
Signals require the meta-object system: a hub class missing Q_OBJECT (or moc) quietly offers no signals and fails later with a missing-vtable link error.
Qt signals do not return values; a mediator that needs a reply must model it as another signal or a QFuture, never as a return type.
